{"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1NjU5NTg=","is_bot":false,"login":"gregce","name":"Greg Ceccarelli"},"body":"## Summary\n\nOn macOS, `specstory watch` fsnotify-watches every `YYYY/MM/DD` directory under `~/.codex/sessions`, including all history. fsnotify's kqueue backend must hold an open fd for every file in a watched directory, so a single watch process pins roughly one fd per rollout file ever written. Watching historical directories buys nothing: those files are immutable and never fire events.\n\n## Impact\n\nMeasured on an install with ~25,400 rollout files: **25,459 open fds per `watch` process** (`lsof`, plain REG entries with `O_EVTONLY`). Multiple watch processes multiply this; 13 accumulated processes held ~359k of the 368,640 system-wide ceiling (`sysctl kern.maxfiles`), at which point every process on the machine fails with \"too many open files in system.\"\n\nDiagnose with:\n\n```sh\nsysctl kern.num_files          # total fds in use system-wide\nlsof -c specstory | wc -l      # SpecStory's share\n```\n\n## Mechanism\n\n- `startCodexSessionWatcher` (`specstory-cli/pkg/providers/codexcli/watcher.go:156`) walks the full sessions tree at startup and calls `watcher.Add` on the root and every year/month/day dir (`watchYearDir` :257, `watchMonthDir` :227, `watchDayDir` :216). There are no `watcher.Remove` calls; fds release only at process exit.\n- fsnotify's darwin backend opens each watched dir with `O_EVTONLY` and then, via `watchDirectoryFiles` (`backend_kqueue.go:582`), opens one persistent fd per file inside it. This is documented fsnotify behavior on macOS, not a leak in our code (all of our own opens in `pkg/providers/codexcli` have deferred closes).\n\n## Proposed fix\n\nKeep the one-time startup scan of all history (`scanDayDir`) unchanged, but only `watcher.Add` the current date chain (root, current year/month/day) plus the resume session's day dir when `resumeSessionID` is set. The existing Create handler (`watcher.go:353-364`) already picks up new date dirs at rollover; preserve its Add-before-scan ordering (`watchDayDir` adds the watch at :217 before scanning at :223, which closes the mkdir-to-watch race).\n\nExpected result: ~25k fds down to a few dozen per watch process, with identical startup sync output.\n\n## Trade-off to decide\n\nA Codex session resumed directly (outside SpecStory) whose rollout lives in an old day dir would no longer stream live updates, only be caught at the next startup scan. Watching a trailing window (today + N days) reduces this to near zero.\n\n## Related\n\nThe claudecode provider watches the whole `~/.claude/projects/<project>` dir with the same per-file-fd behavior (bounded, but can reach thousands of fds on heavy projects). Same treatment applies as a follow-up.\n","comments":[],"createdAt":"2026-08-02T15:36:49Z","labels":[],"number":266,"state":"OPEN","title":"watch pins one fd per historical Codex rollout file (~25k on large installs) and can exhaust the macOS system fd table"}

127	// dirType determines the type of directory relative to sessionsRoot based on the
128	// YYYY/MM/DD structure. Returns "year", "month", "day", or "" if not a recognized type.
129	func dirType(path string, sessionsRoot string) string {
130		rel, err := filepath.Rel(sessionsRoot, path)
131		if err != nil || strings.HasPrefix(rel, "..") {
132			return "" // Path is not under sessionsRoot
133		}
134	
135		parts := strings.Split(filepath.ToSlash(rel), "/")
136		switch len(parts) {
137		case 1: // YYYY
138			if len(parts[0]) == 4 {
139				return "year"
140			}
141		case 2: // YYYY/MM
142			if len(parts[0]) == 4 && len(parts[1]) == 2 {
143				return "month"
144			}
145		case 3: // YYYY/MM/DD
146			if len(parts[0]) == 4 && len(parts[1]) == 2 && len(parts[2]) == 2 {
147				return "day"
148			}
149		}
150		return ""
151	}

183				}

189	
190			// Helper to add a directory to watcher if not already watched
191			addWatch := func(dir string) error {

193				defer watchedDirsMutex.Unlock()
194	
195				if watchedDirs[dir] {
196					return nil // Already watching
197				}
198	
199				if err := watcher.Add(dir); err != nil {
200					return err
201				}

203				slog.Info("startCodexSessionWatcher: Added watch", "directory", dir)
204				return nil
205			}

207			// Helper to scan a day directory for existing sessions
208			scanDayDir := func(dayDir string) {

214

218					slog.Error("startCodexSessionWatcher: Failed to watch day directory",

221					return

223				scanDayDir(dayDir)

225	
226			// Helper to watch a month directory and its existing day directories
227			watchMonthDir := func(monthDir string) {

235				// Scan for existing day directories
236				entries, err := os.ReadDir(monthDir)

239						"directory", monthDir,
240						"error", err)
241					return
242				}
243	
244				for _, entry := range entries {
245					if !entry.IsDir() {
246						continue
247					}
248					// Day directories are named 01-31
249					if len(entry.Name()) == 2 {

252					}
253				}
254			}
255	
256			// Helper to watch a year directory and its existing month directories
257			watchYearDir := func(yearDir string) {
258				if err := addWatch(yearDir); err != nil {

262					return
263				}
264	
265				// Scan for existing month directories
266				entries, err := os.ReadDir(yearDir)

273	
274				for _, entry := range entries {

283				}
284			}
285	
286			// Watch sessions root for year directories

302						continue
303					}

317			for {

319				case <-watcherCtx.Done():
320					slog.Info("startCodexSessionWatcher: Context cancelled, stopping watcher")
321					return
322	
323				case event, ok := <-watcher.Events:
324					if !ok {
325						slog.Info("startCodexSessionWatcher: Watcher events channel closed")
326						return
327					}
328	
329					if !event.Has(fsnotify.Create) && !event.Has(fsnotify.Write) && !event.Has(fsnotify.Remove) {

333					// Determine what type of path this is

347							ScanCodexSessions(projectPath, parentDir, nil)
348						}
349						continue
350					}
351	
352					// Check if this is a directory creation
353					if event.Has(fsnotify.Create) {
354						switch dirType(eventPath, sessionsRoot) {
355						case "year":
356							slog.Info("startCodexSessionWatcher: New year directory created", "directory", eventPath)
357							watchYearDir(eventPath)
358						case "month":

365					}

367				case err, ok := <-watcher.Errors:

372					log.UserWarn("Watcher error: %v", err)

381	// ScanCodexSessions scans JSONL files in the session directory and processes sessions
382	// that match the project path. If changedFile is nil, scans all JSONL files in the directory.
383	// If changedFile is non-nil, only processes that specific file.
384	func ScanCodexSessions(projectPath string, sessionDir string, changedFile *string) {
385		// Ensure logs are flushed even if we panic
386		defer func() {
387			if r := recover(); r != nil {
388				log.UserWarn("PANIC in ScanCodexSessions: %v", r)
389				slog.Error("ScanCodexSessions: PANIC recovered", "panic", r)
390			}
391		}()
392	
393		slog.Info("ScanCodexSessions: === START SCAN ===", "timestamp", time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339))
394		if changedFile != nil {
395			slog.Info("ScanCodexSessions: Scanning with changed file",
396				"projectPath", projectPath,
397				"sessionDir", sessionDir,
398				"changedFile", *changedFile)
399		} else {
400			slog.Info("ScanCodexSessions: Scanning all sessions",
401				"projectPath", projectPath,
402				"sessionDir", sessionDir)
403		}
404	
405		// Get the session callback
406		callback := getWatcherCallback()
407		if callback == nil {
408			slog.Error("ScanCodexSessions: No callback provided - this should not happen")
409			return
410		}
411	
412		// Normalize project path for comparison
413		normalizedProjectPath := normalizeCodexPath(projectPath)
414		if normalizedProjectPath == "" {
415			slog.Debug("ScanCodexSessions: Unable to normalize project path", "projectPath", projectPath)
416		}
417	
418		// If we have a specific changed file, only process that file
419		if changedFile != nil {
420			if err := processCodexSessionFile(*changedFile, projectPath, normalizedProjectPath, callback); err != nil {
421				slog.Debug("ScanCodexSessions: Failed to process changed file",
422					"file", *changedFile,
423					"error", err)
424			}
425			slog.Info("ScanCodexSessions: === END SCAN ===", "timestamp", time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339))
426			return
427		}
428	
429		// Otherwise, scan all JSONL files in the session directory
430		entries, err := os.ReadDir(sessionDir)
431		if err != nil {
432			slog.Error("ScanCodexSessions: Failed to read session directory",
433				"directory", sessionDir,
434				"error", err)
435			return
436		}
437	
438		for _, entry := range entries {
439			if entry.IsDir() {
440				continue
441			}
442			if filepath.Ext(entry.Name()) != ".jsonl" {
443				continue
444			}
445	
446			sessionPath := filepath.Join(sessionDir, entry.Name())
447			if err := processCodexSessionFile(sessionPath, projectPath, normalizedProjectPath, callback); err != nil {
448				slog.Debug("ScanCodexSessions: Failed to process session file",
449					"file", sessionPath,
450					"error", err)
451				// Continue processing other files even if one fails
452			}
453		}
454	
455		slog.Info("ScanCodexSessions: Processing complete")
456		slog.Info("ScanCodexSessions: === END SCAN ===", "timestamp", time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339))
457	}

459	// processCodexSessionFile processes a single Codex session file and calls the callback
460	// if the session matches the project path.
461	func processCodexSessionFile(sessionPath string, projectPath string, normalizedProjectPath string, callback func(*spi.AgentChatSession)) error {
462		// Load session metadata
463		meta, err := loadCodexSessionMeta(sessionPath)
464		if err != nil {
465			return fmt.Errorf("failed to load session meta: %w", err)
466		}
467	
468		// Check if session matches project path
469		sessionID := strings.TrimSpace(meta.Payload.ID)
470		normalizedCWD := normalizeCodexPath(meta.Payload.CWD)
471		if normalizedCWD == "" {
472			slog.Debug("processCodexSessionFile: Session meta missing cwd", "sessionID", sessionID, "path", sessionPath)
473			return fmt.Errorf("session meta missing cwd")
474		}
475	
476		// Check if this session matches the project path
477		matched := false
478		if normalizedProjectPath != "" {
479			if normalizedCWD == normalizedProjectPath || strings.EqualFold(normalizedCWD, normalizedProjectPath) {
480				matched = true
481			}
482		} else if normalizedCWD == projectPath || strings.EqualFold(normalizedCWD, projectPath) {
483			matched = true
484		}
485	
486		if !matched {
487			slog.Debug("processCodexSessionFile: Session does not match project path",
488				"sessionID", sessionID,
489				"sessionCWD", normalizedCWD,
490				"projectPath", normalizedProjectPath)
491			return nil // Not an error, just doesn't match
492		}
493	
494		slog.Info("processCodexSessionFile: Session matched project",
495			"sessionID", sessionID,
496			"sessionPath", sessionPath)
497	
498		// Create session info
499		sessionInfo := &codexSessionInfo{
500			SessionID:   sessionID,
501			SessionPath: sessionPath,
502			Meta:        meta,
503		}
504	
505		// Process the session
506		agentSession, err := processSessionToAgentChat(sessionInfo, projectPath, getWatcherDebugRaw())
507		if err != nil {
508			return fmt.Errorf("failed to process session: %w", err)
509		}
510	
511		// Skip empty sessions
512		if agentSession == nil {
513			slog.Debug("processCodexSessionFile: Skipping empty session", "sessionID", sessionID)
514			return nil
515		}
516	
517		// Skip sessions without user message (empty slug)
518		if agentSession.Slug == "" {
519			slog.Debug("processCodexSessionFile: Skipping session without user message",
520				"sessionID", agentSession.SessionID)
521			return nil
522		}

I've verified the issue against the code — everything in the report checks out. Here's my analysis and recommendation.

## What I confirmed

The issue (filed by Greg) is accurate on all points:

- `startCodexSessionWatcher` in `pkg/providers/codexcli/watcher.go:156` walks the entire `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD` tree at startup and calls `watcher.Add` on the root and every year, month, and day directory (`watchYearDir` → `watchMonthDir` → `watchDayDir`). There is not a single `watcher.Remove` in the codexcli provider, so watches only release at process exit.
- On macOS, fsnotify's kqueue backend must hold an open fd for the directory *and every file inside it* for each watched directory. This is documented fsnotify behavior, not a bug in our code. So the fd count scales with the total number of rollout files ever written — ~25k fds per process on the reporter's install.
- Watching historical day dirs buys nothing in the common case: those rollout files are immutable. The only reason we touch them at startup is the initial scan (`scanDayDir` → `ScanCodexSessions`), which reads them once and needs no watch.
- Both entry points funnel through this code: `specstory run` (`ExecAgentAndWatch`, `provider.go:403`) and the long-running `specstory watch` (`WatchAgent`, `provider.go:452`). Multiple concurrent processes multiply the fd load, which is how the reporter hit the system-wide `kern.maxfiles` ceiling.

One structural detail matters for the fix: today, scanning and watching are fused — `watchDayDir` adds the watch and then scans. The fix needs to decouple them so we still scan all history at startup (preserving identical sync output) while only watching a small set of directories.

## Options

**Option 1 — Watch only the current date chain (the issue's minimal proposal).**
Watch the sessions root, current year, current month, current day, plus the resume session's day dir when `--resume` is used. The existing Create handler (`watcher.go:353-364`) already handles date rollover — a new day/month/year dir created under a watched parent gets picked up, and its Add-before-scan ordering already closes the mkdir-to-watch race.

- Pros: smallest change, ~25k fds drops to a few dozen, no behavior change to startup sync.
- Cons: a Codex session started yesterday but still active (spanning midnight), or one resumed outside SpecStory via plain `codex resume` into an old day dir, won't stream live — it's only caught at the next startup scan.

**Option 2 — Option 1 plus a small trailing window (today + previous 1–2 days).**
Same as above, but also watch day dirs from the last day or two.

- Pros: same fd reduction to within rounding error (a couple dozen extra fds). Closes the midnight-spanning gap and covers most out-of-band resumes, since resumed-session activity overwhelmingly targets recent sessions. Cost is trivially small.
- Cons: slightly more logic (a date-window predicate), and it's a heuristic — a session resumed from three weeks ago still won't stream live.

**Option 3 — Switch macOS to an FSEvents-based watcher.**
FSEvents watches trees recursively without per-file fds, which would eliminate the problem class entirely.

- Pros: structurally immune; would also fix the claudecode provider's (bounded but real) version of this.
- Cons: fsnotify mainline doesn't support FSEvents; this means a new dependency (`fsnotify/fsevents`), macOS/Linux code divergence, and a rewrite of battle-tested watcher logic across providers. Way out of proportion to the problem.

## My recommendation: Option 2

Watch the root + current year/month/day chain, the previous ~2 days' day dirs, and the resume session's day dir; keep the full-history startup scan exactly as-is by decoupling "scan" from "watch" in the startup walk. The event handler stays untouched.

Why: Option 1 alone fixes the fd exhaustion but introduces a real (if narrow) live-streaming regression for sessions spanning midnight — which is exactly when a long `specstory watch` is most likely to be running. The trailing window eliminates that for a handful of extra fds and maybe 15 lines of code. The remaining gap (live-streaming a weeks-old session resumed outside SpecStory) is obscure, self-heals at the next startup scan, and Greg's issue explicitly blesses this trade-off. I'd skip adding `watcher.Remove` for aged-out day dirs — a long-lived watch accumulates one day dir per day, which is negligible, and removal logic adds failure modes for no practical gain.

Two things I'd scope separately:

1. **The claudecode provider follow-up.** It watches the whole `~/.claude/projects/<project>` dir with the same per-file-fd behavior. It's bounded per-project rather than unbounded-across-history, so it's lower severity, but on heavy projects (yours would qualify) it's thousands of fds. Same treatment applies; I'd file it as its own issue as Greg suggests. It's also worth a `/symmetry-audit` pass afterward — `droidcli`, `geminicli`, `deepseektui`, and `antigravitycli` all call `watcher.Add` too, though at a quick glance they watch single flat dirs, so they're likely fine.
2. **The "13 accumulated watch processes" detail.** That's a second smell hiding in the repro: something left 13 `specstory` watch processes alive on the reporter's machine. The fd fix shrinks each process's footprint ~1000x, which defuses the systemic blast radius, but if watch processes are failing to exit somewhere, that's an independent bug worth understanding. The issue doesn't cover why they accumulated.

Implementation-wise it's a contained change to `startCodexSessionWatcher`: extract a `shouldWatchDir` predicate (pure function over path + date window + resume dir, unit-testable table-style alongside the existing `dirType` tests), have the startup walk always scan day dirs but only conditionally add watches, and leave the event-driven rollover path exactly as it is.

Want me to go ahead and implement Option 2 (or Option 1 if you'd rather take the strictly minimal change)?

_**Agent (claude-fable-5 2026-08-03 20:45:28Z)**_

Your instinct is right — the accumulation is real, and it's worth quantifying, because it changes what I'd dismiss as unnecessary complexity.

## How the accumulation plays out

With Option 2 as I sketched it (no `Remove` calls), a long-lived watch gains fds two ways:

1. **One day dir per day** via the rollover Create handler. Each newly watched day dir pins one fd for the dir itself plus one per rollout file inside it, and kqueue picks up new files as they're written into any watched dir.
2. **Nothing else shrinks.** Once watched, a day dir's fds are held until process exit — so the fd count is monotonically increasing, bounded by "every rollout file written during the watch's lifetime."

Concretely: a heavy Codex user writing ~30 rollouts/day, watch alive for 90 days → ~2,700 fds. A year → ~11k. So it doesn't hit the wall in a week, but in extremis it recreates exactly the original problem — just with "history since watch started" substituted for "all history." And with multiple long-lived watch processes (one per project, say), you're multiplying again, which is the same shape as the 13-process incident in the issue. For a feature whose premise is "runs for months," a monotonically-growing fd count is a design bug, not an edge case.

## What I'd change: make the window actually slide

The piece I previously skipped — `watcher.Remove` for aged-out day dirs — becomes justified. The good news is it's cheap and has a natural trigger point:

- When the rollover Create event fires for a new day dir (the handler at `watcher.go:353-364`), after adding the new watch, prune: walk the `watchedDirs` map, and for any *day* dir whose date falls outside the 7-day window, call `watcher.Remove` and delete it from the map. fsnotify's kqueue backend closes the dir fd and all per-file fds on Remove, so the memory and fd footprint both go flat.
- Prune-on-rollover is sufficient — no timer needed. If Codex writes nothing for a week, no new day dir is created, so nothing accumulates and there's nothing urgent to prune; the stale watches just sit until the next day dir appears. Fd usage becomes O(files in the trailing 7 days), constant forever.
- Old month/year dirs can be pruned in the same pass (a January month dir is dead weight once February exists). They're only ~1 fd each plus their handful of child entries, so this is tidiness rather than necessity, but it's two more lines in the same loop.
- Failure handling is benign: `watcher.Remove` on an already-gone dir returns an error you can log-and-ignore, same as the existing claudecode provider does at `watcher.go:175`.

The behavioral trade-off stays the same as the 7-day window itself: a session that's *still actively streaming* when its day dir ages past 7 days would stop streaming live. That requires a single Codex session continuously active for over a week — effectively nil, and the next startup scan catches it.

## One knock-on consequence worth flagging

Long-lived watch makes the **claudecode follow-up more urgent and harder**. The codexcli fix works because history is partitioned by date — we can drop whole directories. Claude Code's `~/.claude/projects/<project>` is one flat dir, so every session file ever written for that project stays pinned as long as the dir is watched, and there's no directory-granularity pruning available. During a months-long watch that grows too (one fd per new session file, plus all historical ones from startup). The mitigations there look different — possibly watching the dir but periodically cycling the watch, or accepting that this is where an FSEvents-based backend earns its keep on macOS. Not something to solve in this PR, but if long-lived watch is the roadmap, that issue should be filed with that framing rather than as a "same treatment" clone.

So, updated recommendation: **Option 2 with a 7-day window and prune-on-rollover** — the sliding window in both directions. That makes fd usage flat regardless of process lifetime, which is the property you actually want for a weeks/months-lived watch.

Want me to implement it that way?

package codexcli

import (
	"path/filepath"
	"testing"
	"time"
)

func TestWatchWindowCutoff(t *testing.T) {
	tests := []struct {
		name     string
		now      time.Time
		expected time.Time
	}{
		{
			name:     "mid-month afternoon truncates to midnight",
			now:      time.Date(2026, 8, 3, 15, 4, 5, 0, time.UTC),
			expected: time.Date(2026, 7, 27, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
		},
		{
			name:     "window spans a year boundary",
			now:      time.Date(2026, 1, 4, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
			expected: time.Date(2025, 12, 28, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
		},
	}

	for _, tt := range tests {
		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			got := watchWindowCutoff(tt.now)
			if !got.Equal(tt.expected) {
				t.Errorf("watchWindowCutoff(%v) = %v, expected %v", tt.now, got, tt.expected)
			}
		})
	}
}

func TestDirWithinWatchWindow(t *testing.T) {
	sessionsRoot := filepath.Join("home", "user", ".codex", "sessions")

	yearBoundaryCutoff := time.Date(2025, 12, 28, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)

_**Agent (claude-fable-5 2026-08-03 20:59:44Z)**_

The fix works — verified live. Here's the summary.

## What I implemented

All changes are in `pkg/providers/codexcli/watcher.go`, plus a new `watcher_test.go` (the test file was part of the approved plan; flagging it since it's a new file).

**The window (`watcher.go`):**

- `watchWindowDays = 7` — a package constant with a comment explaining the kqueue fd rationale, plus two pure helpers: `watchWindowCutoff` (now minus 7 days, truncated to local midnight) and `dirWithinWatchWindow` (decides whether a year/month/day dir could contain sessions on or after the cutoff).
- `watchYearDir`/`watchMonthDir`/`watchDayDir` now consult a `shouldWatch` closure before calling `watcher.Add`, but **always continue recursing and scanning** — so the full-history startup scan (and its sync output) is byte-identical to before. The Add-before-scan ordering that closes the mkdir-to-watch race is preserved for watched dirs.
- **Resume pinning:** `WatchForCodexSessions` now passes the resumed session's day dir down as `pinnedDayDir`; it's watched regardless of age and exempt from pruning, so `specstory run --resume` on an old session streams live for the whole process lifetime.
- **Prune-on-rollover:** when the day-dir Create event fires (the only moment the watched set grows), a `pruneStaleWatches` closure removes watches for any dir that has aged out of the window — day dirs older than 7 days, and month/year dirs once the window no longer reaches into them. `watcher.Remove` failures are logged at debug and ignored (the kernel already released the fds if the dir vanished), matching the claudecode provider's existing pattern.

## Verification

- `golangci-lint run` — 0 issues; `go test ./...` — all packages pass, including the new table-driven tests covering window boundaries, the year-boundary case (cutoff Dec 28 → January dirs kept, November dropped), and malformed paths.
- Live test: built the binary, ran `specstory watch` against your real `~/.codex/sessions` (88 rollout files, 52 date dirs), and checked with `lsof`. The watch process holds **14 fds** under the sessions tree instead of ~140+: the root, the 2026 year dir, the July month dir, and the one in-window day dir (`2026/07/29`) with its single rollout file. Out-of-window dirs like `2026/07/10` show up only as directory-entry fds of their watched parent — their *files* are not pinned, which is exactly the kqueue behavior we're exploiting. The 2025 tree isn't watched at all.

One observation from that run: the process still held ~360 fds total — the remainder is mostly the claudecode provider watching this (large) project's `~/.claude/projects` dir, which is a nice concrete preview of why that follow-up matters. As discussed, that one needs different treatment since its dir is flat.

I haven't committed anything (per your git rules) and haven't commented on issue #266 — let me know if you want a comment drafted for it. Ready to move to the Claude Code follow-up whenever you are.

_**Agent (claude-fable-5 2026-08-03 21:19:31Z)**_

Here's my honest per-item assessment — two are worth taking, two I'd push back on.

## 1. Range validation + round-trip check — agree, cheap and defensible

Right now `dirWithinWatchWindow` inherits `dirType`'s width-only validation, so a dir shaped like `2026/13` or `2026/02/30` passes the shape check and `time.Date` silently normalizes it (month 13 → January next year, Feb 30 → March 2). To be clear about actual exposure: it's theoretical. Codex only creates valid date dirs, and the worst case for a hand-made junk dir is one wasted fd. But the round-trip check (construct the `time.Date`, verify `Year()/Month()/Day()` match the parsed ints) is ~4 lines, makes the pure function correct in isolation rather than correct-given-its-caller, and correctly rejects things like non-leap-year Feb 29. Since this predicate also drives *pruning*, self-contained correctness is worth having.

One asymmetry worth knowing about: the Create-event handler decides via `dirType`, which keeps width-only checks — so a junk-shaped dir created *while watching* would still get watched, then dropped at the next prune. That pre-existing looseness in `dirType` is out of scope, and the asymmetry is harmless.

## 2. Injectable interface for a traversal test — disagree as proposed

This is where I'd push back. The suggestion is the classic "add a seam for testability" move, but look at what's left to test once the predicate is extracted: `shouldWatch` is a two-line closure, and each `watch*Dir` helper is "if shouldWatch → Add (bail on error); recurse/scan regardless." The complicated logic — window math, boundary behavior, path validation — already lives in pure functions with table tests. What the interface would buy is a test that the three-line wiring calls the things it visibly calls, at the cost of permanent indirection in production code whose only consumer is tests. That runs against the project's conventions (simplicity first, don't test tautological things).

There's also a structural obstacle the reviewer likely didn't see: the watcher runs on package-global singletons (`watcherCtx`, `watcherWg`, the callback mutex), and `StopWatcher` cancels a context that's created once in `init()`. A lifecycle test would need that state made re-entrant first — a real refactor of battle-tested code.

Where I *would* revisit: an integration-style test with a real fsnotify watcher over a temp-dir date tree (more aligned with this codebase's style than a mock seam). That becomes worth the singleton refactor when we do the claudecode follow-up, since we'd likely want shared watcher test infrastructure anyway. I'd defer it to that work rather than bolt it onto this change.

## 3. Comment clarification — agree, trivially

The current comment says "days before today" but making "7-day lookback **plus today**, so up to 8 day dirs" explicit removes any off-by-one ambiguity for the next reader. No reason not to.

## 4. Prune tests across month/year boundaries — mostly already covered; remainder is contingent on #2

Worth noting: the boundary *logic* is already tested — the `yearBoundaryCutoff` cases in `watcher_test.go` cover exactly the December-window-into-January scenario (November dropped, December kept, January kept), and pruning is just that predicate plus a loop-and-remove. What's not tested is the loop itself, which has no branches beyond the root/pinned exemptions. So this suggestion collapses into #2: valuable only if the harness from #2 exists, redundant otherwise. Same verdict — defer to the claudecode round.

## Bottom line

Take #1 and #3 now (about 10 lines combined, no behavior change for any real directory); decline #2 and #4 for this change and reconsider them when we refactor for the claudecode follow-up. Want me to apply #1 and #3?

Both applied, linter clean, full test suite passes.

**#3 (comment clarity):** The `watchWindowDays` comment now states explicitly that the window is the 7-day lookback *plus today*, so up to `watchWindowDays+1` day directories are watched at once — no off-by-one ambiguity for the next reader.

**#1 (date validation):** `dirWithinWatchWindow` now rejects components that pass the width check but aren't real calendar dates:

- Month dirs get a simple 1–12 range check (a round-trip would be overkill when the range *is* the validity condition).
- Day dirs get the round-trip check the reviewer suggested: construct the `time.Date`, then verify `Year()/Month()/Day()` match the parsed components. Since `time.Date` normalizes out-of-range values rather than erroring, a mismatch is the signal that the components weren't a real date — that's the "why" comment I left on it. This correctly rejects `13` months, day `32`, Feb 30, and Feb 29 in non-leap years, while accepting Feb 29 in leap years.

Seven new table cases cover exactly those paths (month 13/00, day 32/00, Feb 30, Feb 29 in 2026 vs. 2028), all passing alongside the existing boundary tests. No behavior change for any directory Codex actually creates — this only hardens the predicate against junk-but-date-shaped names.

That closes out the codexcli fix. Everything's uncommitted on `dev` for your review; ready for the claudecode follow-up whenever you want to pick it up.

This provides the same support for saving to local markdown files and to the SpecStory Cloud as for [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/docs/api/claude-code), [Cursor CLI](https://cursor.com/docs/cli), [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli/), Factory's [Droid CLI](https://factory.ai/product/cli), [Cursor IDE](https://cursor.com/product) and [DeepSeek TUI](https://github.com/Hmbown/DeepSeek-TUI).
8	- The [Antigravity CLI](https://antigravity.google/) provider does _not_ support using `specstory resume` to resume other agent's sessions in Antigravity. Resuming Antigravity CLI sessions in other agents is fully supported. This is due to issues with creating the protocol buffer data structures Antigravity uses for session storage.
9	- The [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) provider is now deprecated and will eventually be completely replaced by the [Antigravity CLI](https://antigravity.google/) provider. The Gemini CLI provider remains in place today to help with synchronizing legacy Gemini CLI sessions, and to allow those sessions to be resumed in other agents.
10

12	
13	### ⚙️ Improvements
14	
15	- SpecStory coding agent session histories are now saved by default with secrets redacted via the [Betterleaks](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks) library. Thank you to [warnes](https://github.com/warnes) for the [contribution](https://github.com/specstoryai/getspecstory/pull/235).
16	- Redaction also covers all the data synced to SpecStory Cloud, not just local markdown.

23	
24	- Fixed some indeterminism in Clade Code session rendering order around the Claude `local-command-caveat` that could cause markdown edit churn on repeated `sync` runs.

27	
28	### 📢 Announcements
29	
30	- The SpecStory CLI now supports the [Cursor IDE](https://cursor.com/product) (i.e. `cursoride`) for sessions created from Cursor version 3 or higher. Sessions from earlier versions may work, but are not officially supported. This provides the same support for saving to local markdown files and to the SpecStory Cloud as for [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/docs/api/claude-code), [Cursor CLI](https://cursor.com/docs/cli), [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli/), [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli), Factory's [Droid CLI](https://factory.ai/product/cli), and [DeepSeek TUI](https://github.com/Hmbown/CodeWhale)

34	
35	### 📢 Announcements
36	
37	- [SpecStory Pro](https://specstory.com/pricing) users can now use `specstory resume` to resume agent sessions from other machines using any session that's been synced to their SpecStory Cloud account from any other computer.
38	- [SpecStory Pro](https://specstory.com/pricing) users can now use `specstory search` to search, browse and view agent sessions you've synced to SpecStory Cloud from any other computer.
39	- [SpecStory Pro](https://specstory.com/pricing) users can now use `specstory skills` to generate, review, and install skills forged from the SpecStory histories that are synced to SpecStory Cloud from all their computers.

41	### ⚙️ Improvements
42	
43	- SpecStory CLI operations that use the `~/.specstory/sessions.db` SQLite database (e.g. `specstory reindex`, `specstory search`, `specstory resume`) now self-heal if the `sessions.db` file is removed but the `sessions.db-wal` and/or `session.db-shm` files remain.
44	- More agent sessions from the Cursor CLI provider are now attributed to the correct project in `specstory search` and `specstory resume` and not to an `unknown` project. This is challenging as the Cursor CLI agent session data does not include the project directory, and instead has a one-way hash of the project directory. We know use additional techniques to determine the correct project directory for the session, when it's possible to do so.

55	### 📢 Announcements
56	
57	- The SpecStory CLI now supports cross-project and cross-agent resume using `specstory resume`. Run `specstory resume` in any project dir and by default it shows you all the agent coding sessions for that project across all the supported providers. You can select any session and then select any coding agent you have installed to resume it in. For example, you can resume a Claude Code session in Codex. You can press `tab` in the UI to switch to a project browser and resume sessions from other projects in the current project. You can press `a` in the UI to filter the sessions by type of coding agent. You can pre-select the target agent you'll be resuming into by specifying it with `specstory resume <agent>`.
58	- The SpecStory CLI now supports indexed project and cross-project full-text search of your agent coding sessions using `specstory search`. By default you'll be searching across all projects, and you can limit it to the current project directory with `tab` and filter results to a specific agent with `a`.
59	- The `resume` and `search` features rely on a session index created in `~/.specstory/session.db`. This index is created automatically the first time you run `resume` or `search`, or you can create it manually with `specstory reindex`.

253	// scanJSONLFiles scans JSONL files and optionally filters processing to a specific changed file
254	func scanJSONLFiles(claudeProjectDir string, changedFile ...string) {
255		// Ensure logs are flushed even if we panic
256		defer func() {
257			if r := recover(); r != nil {
258				log.UserWarn("PANIC in ScanJSONLFiles: %v", r)
259				slog.Error("ScanJSONLFiles: PANIC recovered", "panic", r)
260			}
261		}()
262	
263		slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: === START SCAN ===", "timestamp", time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339))
264		var targetFile string
265		if len(changedFile) > 0 && changedFile[0] != "" {
266			targetFile = changedFile[0]

268				"directory", claudeProjectDir,
269				"changedFile", targetFile)
270		} else {
271			slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Scanning JSONL files", "directory", claudeProjectDir)
272		}
273		// Parse files and create history files:

275		var targetSessionUuid string
276	
277		// Set the target file for conditional debug output
278		if targetFile != "" {
279			SetDebugTargetFile(targetFile)
280			defer ClearDebugTargetFile()
281	
282			sessionID, err := extractSessionIDFromFile(targetFile)
283			if err != nil {
284				slog.Warn("ScanJSONLFiles: Failed to extract session ID from file",
285					"file", targetFile,
286					"error", err)
287				slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Skipping scan due to file read error", "file", targetFile)
288				return
289			}
290			if sessionID == "" {
291				slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Skipping scan; session ID not present yet", "file", targetFile)
292				return
293			}
294			targetSessionUuid = sessionID
295			slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Extracted session ID from changed file",
296				"sessionUuid", targetSessionUuid,
297				"file", targetFile)
298		}
299	
300		var parseErr error
301		if targetSessionUuid != "" {
302			parseErr = parser.ParseProjectSessionsForSession(claudeProjectDir, true, targetSessionUuid)
303		} else {
304			parseErr = parser.ParseProjectSessions(claudeProjectDir, true)
305		}
306		if parseErr != nil {
307			log.UserWarn("Error parsing project sessions: %v", parseErr)
308			slog.Error("ScanJSONLFiles: Error parsing project sessions", "error", parseErr)
309			return
310		}
311	
312		// Process JSONL sessions (isAutosave = true, silent = false for autosave)
313		slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Processing sessions",
314			"sessionCount", len(parser.Sessions),
315			"targetSessionUuid", targetSessionUuid)
316	
317		// Get the session callback
318		callback := getWatcherCallback()
319		if callback == nil {
320			slog.Error("ScanJSONLFiles: No callback provided - this should not happen")
321			return
322		}
323	
324		slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Processing sessions with callback")
325		// Process sessions and call the callback for each
326		for _, session := range parser.Sessions {
327			// Skip empty sessions
328			if len(session.Records) == 0 {
329				continue
330			}
331	
332			// Skip if we're targeting a specific session and this isn't it
333			if targetSessionUuid != "" && session.SessionUuid != targetSessionUuid {
334				continue
335			}
336	
337			// Convert to AgentChatSession (workspaceRoot extracted from records' cwd field)
338			agentSession := convertToAgentChatSession(session, "", getWatcherDebugRaw())
339			if agentSession != nil {
340				slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Calling callback for session", "sessionId", agentSession.SessionID)
341				// Call the callback in a goroutine to avoid blocking
342				go func(s *spi.AgentChatSession) {
343					defer func() {
344						if r := recover(); r != nil {
345							slog.Error("ScanJSONLFiles: Callback panicked", "panic", r)
346						}
347					}()
348					callback(s)
349				}(agentSession)
350			}
351		}
352		slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: Processing complete")
353		slog.Info("ScanJSONLFiles: === END SCAN ===", "timestamp", time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339))

494	// Returns nil if the session is warmup-only (no real messages)
495	func convertToAgentChatSession(session Session, workspaceRoot string, debugRaw bool) *spi.AgentChatSession {
496		// Skip empty sessions (no records)
497		if len(session.Records) == 0 {
498			return nil
499		}
500	
501		// Write debug files first (even for warmup-only sessions)
502		_ = make(map[int]int) // recordToFileNumber no longer needed
503		if debugRaw {
504			// Write debug files
505			writeDebugRawFiles(session)
506		}
507	
508		// Filter warmup messages
509		filteredRecords := filterWarmupMessages(session.Records)
510	
511		// Skip if no real messages remain after filtering warmup
512		if len(filteredRecords) == 0 {
513			slog.Debug("Skipping warmup-only session", "sessionId", session.SessionUuid)
514			return nil
515		}
516	
517		// Create session with filtered records
518		filteredSession := Session{
519			SessionUuid: session.SessionUuid,
520			Records:     filteredRecords,
521		}
522	
523		// Get timestamp from root record
524		rootRecord := filteredSession.Records[0]
525		timestamp, ok := rootRecord.Data["timestamp"].(string)
526		if !ok {
527			slog.Warn("convertToAgentChatSession: No timestamp found in root record")
528			return nil
529		}
530	
531		// Get the slug
532		slug := FileSlugFromRootRecord(filteredSession)
533	
534		// Generate SessionData from filtered session
535		sessionData, err := GenerateAgentSession(filteredSession, workspaceRoot)
536		if err != nil {
537			slog.Error("Failed to generate SessionData", "sessionId", session.SessionUuid, "error", err)
538			return nil
539		}
540	
541		// Convert session records to JSONL format for raw data
542		// Note: Uses unfiltered session.Records (not filteredSession.Records) to preserve
543		// all records including warmup messages in the raw data for complete audit trail
544		var rawDataBuilder strings.Builder
545		for _, record := range session.Records {
546			jsonBytes, _ := json.Marshal(record.Data)
547			rawDataBuilder.Write(jsonBytes)
548			rawDataBuilder.WriteString("\n")
549		}
550	
551		return &spi.AgentChatSession{
552			SessionID:   session.SessionUuid,
553			CreatedAt:   timestamp, // ISO 8601 timestamp
554			Slug:        slug,
555			SessionData: sessionData,
556			RawData:     rawDataBuilder.String(),
557		}
558	}

_**Agent (claude-fable-5 2026-08-03 21:56:13Z)**_

Here's the full picture, grounded in the code and your actual data.

## What the issue is, exactly

The claudecode watcher (`pkg/providers/claudecode/watcher.go`) watches exactly **one** directory: `~/.claude/projects/<munged-project-path>/` (`startProjectWatcher`, the `watcher.Add` at `watcher.go:203`). That sounds minimal — and on Linux it is. But Claude Code stores sessions as a **flat directory** of `<session-uuid>.jsonl` files, one per session ever run in that project, and on macOS fsnotify's kqueue backend must open one persistent fd for *every file inside* a watched directory to detect writes. So that single legitimate-looking `Add` pins one fd per historical session file. And because kqueue also opens an fd for each *new* file created in the watched dir, the count grows by one per new Claude session and never shrinks — the same monotonic-growth property the Codex watcher had.

There's also a minor cousin: `WatchForClaudeSetup` watches `$HOME` itself when `~/.claude` doesn't exist yet (`watcher.go:402`), which briefly pins an fd per file in your home directory. It's fresh-install-only and transient, so it's a footnote, not the problem.

## How it manifests

On your machine right now, this repo's project dir holds 194 files, so every `specstory run` you start in `specstory-cli` holds ~194 fds for the lifetime of the session — that's most of the ~360 total fds we saw in the live test earlier. Heavy Claude Code users have project dirs with thousands of sessions. The multiplier is worse than Codex in one respect: `specstory run` is per-terminal, and running Claude in three tabs on the same big project means three processes each pinning the full set. It contributes the same system-wide fd-table pressure as issue #266, just with a per-project bound instead of no bound.

## Similar vs. different from the Codex fix

**Same:** identical root cause (kqueue's per-file fds), identical waste (~all pinned files are immutable historical sessions that will never fire an event), identical desired end-state (fds proportional to *recently active* sessions, flat over time).

**Different in the way that matters:** Codex partitions history into `YYYY/MM/DD` directories, so the whole fix was *choosing which directories to Add* — the watch granularity we needed already existed in the filesystem layout. Claude Code's dir is flat. There is no sub-directory to decline to watch; the per-file fds come from the one dir watch itself, and fsnotify gives us no way to say "watch this dir shallowly" or to drop its internally-opened file fds. So the Codex technique has no direct analog — we have to change *what kind of thing* we watch, not which dirs. Two smaller differences: this watcher does no startup scan (initial sync happens in the command layer), which actually simplifies things, and old Claude session files are immutable in practice since resuming a session writes a new UUID file rather than appending to the old one.

## Fix options

**Option A — per-file watches for recent sessions + cheap create-polling on the dir.** Stop `Add`-ing the project dir entirely. Instead: individually `watcher.Add` each `.jsonl` whose mtime falls inside a trailing window (fsnotify happily watches single files at one fd each, delivering Write/Remove/Rename), and detect *new* session files with a periodic `os.ReadDir` name-diff of the project dir — a ticker every ~2 seconds, no per-file stats needed, microseconds of work even at thousands of entries. New file appears → add watch, scan it. On each tick, prune watches on files that aged out. Result: fds ≈ sessions touched in the window (your busiest dir: 0 in the last 7 days versus 194 pinned today).

- Pros: no new dependencies, no platform forks, works identically on Linux, fd usage flat forever, writes still stream in true real-time once a file is watched.
- Cons: new-session *detection* latency of up to one poll interval — invisible in practice, since the first markdown write for a new session trails the first user message anyway. And it's a hybrid push/poll design, slightly less pure than event-only.

**Option B — FSEvents backend on macOS.** The Apple-native API watches trees recursively with essentially zero fds; this is the "eliminates the problem class" fix I mentioned earlier.

- Pros: structurally immune, real-time creates, would eventually fix every provider at once.
- Cons: the maintained binding (`fsnotify/fsevents`) requires **cgo**, which would complicate your cross-compiled release builds; it's a new dependency plus a darwin/linux code fork in the watch layer. Heavy machinery.

**Option C — raw kqueue.** kqueue *can* watch just a directory's entry-list with a single fd (per-file fds are fsnotify's implementation choice for write detection). Hand-rolled kqueue via `x/sys/unix`: one dir fd for creates, per-file fds only for active files.

- Pros: real-time creates without polling, no cgo.
- Cons: we'd own low-level, darwin-specific event-handling code and re-solve edge cases fsnotify solved years ago. High maintenance cost for marginal gain over A.

## My recommendation: Option A

It hits the actual goal — fd usage proportional to active work, flat regardless of process lifetime — with zero new dependencies, no cgo risk to the release pipeline, and one uniform code path for both supported platforms. Its only concession versus B/C is ~2 seconds of latency on detecting a brand-new session file, which no user can observe given that write events (the thing that makes live markdown feel live) remain fully event-driven. I'd use the same 7-day window constant for consistency with the Codex fix, though honestly even a 24-hour window would be defensible here since Claude Code doesn't append to old files.

If you later decide long-lived watch across many providers justifies it, Option B is the strategic endgame — but I'd only take on cgo when there's evidence Option A's shape is insufficient, and nothing here suggests it will be.

_**Agent (claude-fable-5 2026-08-03 22:12:17Z)**_

You're right, and the point cuts deeper than the window size. I was implicitly modeling session files as "written continuously while active, then done" — but a long-running session (an agent on a loop, a session left open over a weekend, multi-day autonomous work) can go quiet for a day-plus and then start writing again. Under a 24h mtime window that session gets pruned while still alive.

And notice what that exposes about Option A's design: the failure isn't just "reduced coverage," it's *unrecoverable within the process*. The ReadDir name-diff only detects **new** files. Writes to an existing-but-unwatched file are invisible — no event fires, and nothing ever re-adds the watch. A pruned-but-still-active session silently stops streaming until the next process restart. That's a worse failure mode than the Codex equivalent, where the day-dir structure meant anything current was in a watched dir by construction.

So two changes to the proposal:

1. **7-day window, full stop** — parity with the Codex fix, and it makes "session idle longer than the window" genuinely exotic rather than merely uncommon.
2. **Make pruning self-healing rather than permanent.** On a slower tick (say every 30–60 seconds, separate from the ~2s create-poll), stat the `.jsonl` files that *aren't* currently watched and re-add any whose mtime has moved. A stat sweep of even a few-thousand-file dir is sub-millisecond, so this costs nothing. With that in place, the window only bounds *fd count*; it never permanently loses a session. Worst case for a session that wakes after any amount of dormancy: live streaming resumes within one slow tick, and the triggering write itself isn't lost because the re-add path scans the file just like a watch event would.

With those two together, the window size stops being a correctness parameter at all — even a session dormant for a month self-heals in under a minute — and 7 days is just the fd/precision knob, consistent with codexcli.

package claudecode

import (
	"sort"
	"testing"
	"time"
)

func TestReconcileFileWatches(t *testing.T) {
	cutoff := time.Date(2026, 7, 27, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
	recent := cutoff.Add(24 * time.Hour)
	old := cutoff.Add(-24 * time.Hour)

	tests := []struct {
		name           string
		files          map[string]time.Time
		watched        map[string]bool
		expectedAdd    []string
		expectedRemove []string
	}{
		{
			name:           "empty directory and nothing watched",
			files:          map[string]time.Time{},
			watched:        map[string]bool{},
			expectedAdd:    nil,
			expectedRemove: nil,
		},
		{
			name: "startup: recent files gain watches, old files do not",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/recent-a.jsonl": recent,
				"/p/recent-b.jsonl": recent,
				"/p/old.jsonl":      old,
			},
			watched:        map[string]bool{},
			expectedAdd:    []string{"/p/recent-a.jsonl", "/p/recent-b.jsonl"},
			expectedRemove: nil,
		},
		{
			name: "steady state: watched recent files stay, nothing changes",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/recent.jsonl": recent,
				"/p/old.jsonl":    old,
			},
			watched:        map[string]bool{"/p/recent.jsonl": true},
			expectedAdd:    nil,
			expectedRemove: nil,
		},
		{
			name: "new session file appears",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/existing.jsonl": recent,
				"/p/new.jsonl":      recent,
			},
			watched:        map[string]bool{"/p/existing.jsonl": true},
			expectedAdd:    []string{"/p/new.jsonl"},
			expectedRemove: nil,
		},
		{
			name: "self-heal: dormant file woken by a write regains its watch",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/woken.jsonl": recent,
			},
			watched:        map[string]bool{},
			expectedAdd:    []string{"/p/woken.jsonl"},
			expectedRemove: nil,
		},
		{
			name: "prune: watched file aged past the cutoff",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/idle.jsonl": old,
			},
			watched:        map[string]bool{"/p/idle.jsonl": true},
			expectedAdd:    nil,
			expectedRemove: []string{"/p/idle.jsonl"},
		},
		{
			name:  "prune: watched file deleted from disk",
			files: map[string]time.Time{},
			watched: map[string]bool{
				"/p/deleted.jsonl": true,
			},
			expectedAdd:    nil,
			expectedRemove: []string{"/p/deleted.jsonl"},
		},
		{
			name: "mtime exactly at cutoff stays watched",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/boundary.jsonl": cutoff,
			},
			watched:        map[string]bool{"/p/boundary.jsonl": true},
			expectedAdd:    nil,
			expectedRemove: nil,
		},
		{
			name: "mixed: add, keep, prune, and delete in one pass",
			files: map[string]time.Time{
				"/p/new.jsonl":   recent,
				"/p/kept.jsonl":  recent,
				"/p/aging.jsonl": old,
			},
			watched: map[string]bool{
				"/p/kept.jsonl":    true,
				"/p/aging.jsonl":   true,
				"/p/deleted.jsonl": true,
			},
			expectedAdd:    []string{"/p/new.jsonl"},
			expectedRemove: []string{"/p/aging.jsonl", "/p/deleted.jsonl"},
		},
	}

	for _, tt := range tests {
		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			add, remove := reconcileFileWatches(tt.files, tt.watched, cutoff)

			// Map iteration order is random, so compare sorted
			sort.Strings(add)
			sort.Strings(remove)

			if !equalStringSlices(add, tt.expectedAdd) {
				t.Errorf("add = %v, expected %v", add, tt.expectedAdd)
			}
			if !equalStringSlices(remove, tt.expectedRemove) {
				t.Errorf("remove = %v, expected %v", remove, tt.expectedRemove)
			}
		})
	}
}

// equalStringSlices compares two string slices treating nil and empty as equal
func equalStringSlices(a, b []string) bool {
	if len(a) != len(b) {
		return false
	}
	for i := range a {
		if a[i] != b[i] {
			return false
		}
	}
	return true
}

_**Agent (claude-fable-5 2026-08-03 22:18:14Z)**_

Done and verified. Here's the summary.

## What changed

All in `pkg/providers/claudecode/watcher.go`, plus a new `watcher_test.go`:

- **No more directory watch.** `startProjectWatcher` never adds the project directory to fsnotify. Instead it maintains a `watchedFiles` set of individually-watched session files — one fd each — for files whose mtime falls within a 7-day window (`watchWindowDays`, with a comment explaining the flat-directory/kqueue rationale and why this provider's shape differs from codexcli's).
- **A single reconcile pass, every 2 seconds** (`watchReconcileInterval`), does all three jobs: lists the directory, and converges the watched set via the pure `reconcileFileWatches(files, watched, cutoff)` function — new files gain watches (create detection), watched files that aged out or were deleted lose them (prune), and dormant files whose mtime moved regain them (**self-heal**). Any watch added *after* startup is immediately scanned, since a watch appearing mid-run means activity happened while unwatched and produced no event. Watch-then-scan ordering closes the gap race, same discipline as the codexcli fix.
- **Startup parity preserved:** the initial reconcile adds watches without scanning — the old dir-watch also generated no scans until the first event, and startup sync remains the command layer's job. Write events on watched files flow through the existing `scanJSONLFiles` path unchanged. Remove/Rename events just drop map entries so a same-named successor gets re-added by reconcile.

The setup-watcher chain (`WatchForClaudeSetup`, parent-dir waiting) is untouched — transient and bounded, as discussed.

## Verification

- Lint clean; full test suite passes. The new table-driven tests cover startup selection, new-file appearance, self-heal, age-out prune, deleted-file prune, the exact-cutoff boundary, and a mixed pass.
- Live test against your real data: this project's Claude dir has 118 session files, 7 modified in the last week. The watch process held exactly **7 fds** there (previously ~119). Dropping a new `.jsonl` into the dir got it watched within one tick, confirming create-detection works end to end. Total process fds are now 180, versus ~361 before either fix.

Changelog got a second bullet under v2.6.0 mirroring the Codex one, including the self-heal guarantee ("resumes live markdown updates within seconds") since that's the user-visible promise.

One honest caveat: the 2-second reconcile means new-session detection is polled, not evented — I verified the mechanism live with a synthetic file, but it's worth a real smoke test on your side: `./specstory watch` in one terminal, start a fresh `claude` session in another, and confirm markdown appears. Everything's uncommitted for your review, alongside the codexcli changes.
